channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Molecular glues: Unlocking new targets in cancer
item.description: The human genome encodes several hundred E3 ligases—the enzymes that decide which proteins a cell destroys. Drug developers have so far harnessed a small number of them. In a new review in Molecular Cell, researchers at Karolinska Institutet and the University of Verona argue that the rest of these E3 ligases are where the next generation of cancer drugs will be found.

item.title: Why older adults take longer to bounce back—and what to do about it
item.description: A class of fatty acid molecules called prostaglandins may be responsible for why older adults often fail to recover muscle strength after illness or injury, while young adults quickly bounce back, a new study has found. Produced by nondividing "zombie cells" called senescent cells, excessive prostaglandins promote muscle atrophy.

item.title: Research team finds an antibody that recognizes DNA shape and responds to antibiotic-induced structural changes
item.description: DNA aptamers are attracting attention as alternatives to antibodies in biosensing and diagnostics. Yet little is known about whether antibodies themselves can recognize the folded structures of DNA aptamers. Researchers at Saitama University have now identified a VHH antibody that preferentially binds an oxytetracycline-associated DNA aptamer.

item.title: Continuing advanced therapies before elective Crohn's surgery may reduce serious complications
item.description: Patients with Crohn's disease who continue advanced therapies, including biologics and small-molecule drugs, in the months before elective colorectal surgery may have a lower risk of two postoperative complications: anastomotic leak and organ space surgical site infection, according to a study published in the Journal of the American College of Surgeons.

item.title: Beyond the shoe: The overlooked role of running socks in foot protection
item.description: For many runners, socks may seem less important than shoes, insoles or training devices. However, as the layer in direct contact with the skin, running socks play an essential role in comfort, impact protection and injury prevention.

item.title: Changes in the heart's electrical signals anticipate the most severe arrhythmias in heart failure patients
item.description: The heart gives warning signs. It does so through small electrical variations—signals so subtle that until now they have gone unnoticed among the millions of data points generated by implantable defibrillators. Today, thanks to remote analysis of the cardiac signal, these whispers can become an early warning.

item.title: South Korea confirms its first case of cholera in 10 years
item.description: South Korea on Friday reported its first case of cholera in 10 years, with health authorities urging people to take precautionary measures, use only safe water and wash their food properly.

item.title: Singapore sees 65% decline in cervical cancer mortality rate since 1990, but screening gaps remain
item.description: Cervical cancer remains one of the few cancers that can potentially be eliminated through human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination, regular screening and timely treatment of precancerous changes. Despite the availability of effective prevention and treatment measures, global deaths from cervical cancer are projected to increase by nearly 40% by 2050, according to a study involving researchers from the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (NUS Medicine) and the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) at the University of Washington.

item.title: Over half of NHS hospitals putting vulnerable patients in public areas, data reveal
item.description: Exclusive data published by The BMJ today reveal that half of hospital trusts in England are breaching NHS corridor care guidelines by treating vulnerable groups in emergency department corridors, including children, mental health patients and those with physical and learning disabilities.

item.title: Paramedics need time and support to recover between emergency calls
item.description: When a paramedic arrives at your door, they may have come straight from someone else's emergency. "I don't know how you do your job," people often tell me. I think about how little time there can be to take in what's happened on one call before the next one comes in.

item.title: Pennsylvania logs another measles death as survey finds few Americans fully understand the disease's risks
item.description: Many Americans are confused about the risks of measles, as well as the safety and benefits of childhood vaccines, according to a survey of more than 1,000 adults released today by the Annenberg Public Policy Center at the University of Pennsylvania.

item.title: At least 178 pregnant Americans have been infected with measles since 2025
item.description: The young woman had weathered a measles infection during pregnancy and recovered—something to celebrate, given the dangers that the virus poses to expectant mothers and babies.

item.title: Wearable heart monitor moves from lab to clinical trial
item.description: A new lightweight, gel-free and waterproof heart monitor that provides real-time insights into heart health is being trialed at an Australian clinic. Originally invented through research at RMIT University and now being developed by Australian startup Lubdub, the wearable wireless patch continuously tracks the heart's rhythm for up to 14 days—giving doctors the same detailed information as a medical-grade electrocardiogram (ECG) Holter monitor.

item.title: New state-by-state scorecard reveals wide gaps in access to obesity treatments
item.description: Where Americans live can make a profound difference in their ability to access obesity treatment, according to a new state-by-state scorecard and report that gives 20 states D or F grades and finds significant barriers to care in every state in the nation.

item.title: ChatGPT's translation of mental health questionnaires into Mandarin reveals inconsistent results
item.description: As more Asian New Zealanders report experiencing mental health challenges, a Te Whare Wānanga o Waitaha | University of Canterbury (UC) researcher is asking a critical question: Can artificial intelligence (AI) help bridge language barriers when human translation resources are limited?

item.title: 'Just one more episode'? How to keep digital distractions from stealing your sleep
item.description: It's happened to us all: You're poised to go to sleep, but a "digital distraction" keeps you up hours later than planned.

item.title: International report discusses risks of chemicals in everyday items
item.description: Two University of Massachusetts Amherst researchers made significant contributions to a new report—more than 10 years in the making—from the United Nations Environment Program (UNEP) and the World Health Organization (WHO) that finds hormone-disrupting chemicals are a "global and growing threat" to human health and the environment.

item.title: Anti-inflammatory peptide shows potential to prevent diabetes-related vision loss
item.description: According to a study published in October in the journal Biomedicine & Pharmacotherapy, a molecule naturally produced by the human body may help protect vision against damage caused by high blood sugar. This finding paves the way for new strategies to prevent diabetic retinopathy. This complication affects more than 22% of people with diabetes worldwide. It occurs when high blood sugar levels cause inflammation and damage neurons and blood vessels in the retina, which can lead to permanent vision loss.

item.title: Nicotine and tobacco smoke damage cells involved in tissue repair
item.description: Nicotine pouches can expose the oral mucosa to high local concentrations of nicotine. A study by the University of Oulu shows that nicotine and tobacco smoke have harmful effects on cells that play a key role in tissue regeneration and wound healing. The findings, published in the Archives of Toxicology, shed light on how nicotine products may compromise oral health and the body's ability to repair damaged tissue.

item.title: Improved blood test offers less invasive way to detect Alzheimer's disease
item.description: A new study in Nature Aging from Lund University in Sweden shows that improved blood tests for the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease can now be used with accuracy similar to that of the cerebrospinal fluid tests that have long been the standard in health care. The blood test has been approved for use in Europe, the U.S. and Japan, among other places. The researchers hope that doctors will now gradually be able to use it more widely—and that, in many cases, patients will be able to avoid the more invasive cerebrospinal fluid test.

item.title: Outside stressors for military members can cause more medical visits
item.description: A new University of Massachusetts Amherst and Naval Health Research Center–led study of more than 34,000 active-duty U.S. military members enrolled in the U.S. Millennium Cohort Study finds those dealing with stress beyond their roles in the service tend to utilize health care more often.

item.title: How the brain builds the present through the lens of the past
item.description: Why does the same sensory stimulus sometimes feel different depending on what came before it? In a study published in Science Advances, a team of neuroscientists at SISSA-Scuola Internazionale Superiore di Studi Avanzati has identified a neural mechanism that helps explain how recent experience shapes present perception: a frontal cortical area carries a memory trace of previous sensory events and combines it with current sensory input.

item.title: New research: Timing of prenatal stress matters for both mothers and infants
item.description: Mental health challenges during pregnancy remain a critical public health issue. As many as 70% of women experience symptoms of stress and anxiety during pregnancy, which can not only affect their own health but also contribute to preterm births, or births before 37 weeks, threatening the health and well-being of infants.

item.title: Study: Seeing social media as having one purpose makes it feel like a better place to reconnect
item.description: You can't be all things to all people, and the same apparently holds true for social media platforms. At its core, social media is supposed to be, well, social. But platforms that do many things at once may feel like an awkward place to reach out to an old friend.

item.title: Seasonal mass vaccination with R21 malaria vaccine effective in reducing malaria infection
item.description: Vaccinating whole communities with the malaria vaccine R21 before the rainy season, alongside existing malaria control tools, can reduce the odds of infection by up to 70%, according to a new study published in The Lancet.

item.title: Where math and language meet: Brain scans reveal shared regions
item.description: Researchers, including those at the University of Tokyo, are helping solve an ongoing debate in the field of neuroscience. Two contradictory positions assume that either math and language are processed in unique areas of the brain, or they are processed together somewhere. Their new research, published in the journal Science Advances, says both are correct in some way: While specialized regions do exist, so does a region newly identified as processing both math and language.

item.title: Cancer cases among trans people could more than double in the next decade, study warns
item.description: A study led by Queen Mary University of London has found that the number of new cancer cases each year among transgender and gender-diverse people in England could more than double over the next decade.

item.title: 'We are finally listening to the experiences of autistic people'
item.description: Dr. Lonnie Zwaigenbaum uses the word "joy" a lot when he talks about autism.

item.title: Lyme disease leaves lasting changes in bone marrow, study finds
item.description: A new study led by researchers at Tufts University School of Medicine suggests that infection with Borrelia burgdorferi, the bacterium that causes Lyme disease, can leave lasting changes in the immune system, even after the infection is treated. The changes occur in the bone marrow, where many of the body's immune cells are made, potentially altering how the immune system responds to future threats.

item.title: Common type 1 diabetes score misses over half of partial remissions in youth with overweight or obesity
item.description: A Baylor College of Medicine–led team is raising awareness about applying the widely used values of insulin dose-adjusted hemoglobin A1c (IDAA1c) when screening for partial type 1 diabetes remission in youth with overweight or obesity. The study appeared in Diabetes Care.
